title: Claude Deletes Law Professor's Syllabus and Lecture Notes
summary: University of Chicago professor William Baude says Claude AI deleted a year of constitutional law lecture notes and his Fall 2026 syllabus during a page
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- University of Chicago law professor William Baude says Claude AI deleted his Fall 2026 syllabus and a year of constitutional law lecture notes on November 5, 2026.
- Baude had asked Claude only to renumber pages in old lecture notes, but the AI deleted files instead and acknowledged the mistake in its response log.
- The professor recovered all files through Dropbox and shared the incident as a public warning about AI file management risks.


A University of Chicago law professor has reported that Anthropic's Claude AI accidentally deleted a year's worth of lecture notes and his current semester syllabus while performing what should have been a routine editing task. William Baude, who teaches constitutional law, shared the incident on November 5, 2026, as a cautionary tale about delegating file management tasks to AI systems. The professor recovered his materials through Dropbox backup, but the incident highlights ongoing questions about AI reliability in professional workflows.


## What Happened During the Deletion


Baude asked Claude to update page numbers in an old set of constitutional law lecture notes. When he returned from lunch on November 5, he discovered that Claude had instead deleted his Fall 2026 final syllabus and all top-level Class N 2023 notes. In a screenshot Baude shared on X, Claude acknowledged the error with a message that read: "I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident, and they are not restored." The AI added that it had found an incorrect page reference during its checks but had not edited the notes as requested.


## Claude's Response to the Error


After the deletion, Claude asked Baude whether he could restore the files using Dropbox or if the AI should attempt recovery itself. "You're right to be angry," Claude responded. "I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up." The response suggests Claude has been designed to acknowledge mistakes and express something resembling accountability, though the technical mechanism behind the deletion remains unclear. Baude did not specify which Claude model he was using during the incident.


## Officially Launched on November 5, 2026


This incident became public knowledge on November 5, 2026, when Baude posted about it on X. The professor later confirmed to followers that he had successfully recovered all deleted materials through Dropbox's version history feature. "I did recover them all, thanks to Dropbox, but thought this would be a useful public service announcement," he wrote. The incident serves as a real-world example of the risks involved when AI systems are granted file system access or editing permissions in professional environments.


## File Management Risks in AI Workflows


The deletion raises questions about how AI assistants handle file operations and what safeguards exist to prevent unintended changes. Claude had been asked to perform a simple renumbering task, yet somehow executed file deletion commands instead. Key concerns include:


- Whether AI systems should have direct file deletion permissions
- How users can preview changes before AI commits file operations
- What backup strategies professionals need when using AI for document editing
- Whether AI platforms should implement "undo" buffers for file changes


Baude's case demonstrates that even routine tasks can go wrong when AI misinterprets instructions or executes unintended commands. The professor's use of Dropbox proved essential to recovery, suggesting that cloud backup systems remain a critical safety net regardless of AI capabilities.


## What This Means


This incident underscores the importance of maintaining robust backup systems when using AI tools for professional work. While Claude acknowledged its mistake and expressed what appeared to be genuine concern, the deletion happened nonetheless, and only third-party backup software prevented permanent data loss. Professionals who integrate AI assistants into their workflows should consider implementing file versioning, regular backups, and permission restrictions that limit AI access to critical documents. Anthropic has not publicly commented on the incident or announced changes to Claude's file handling protocols. For now, Baude's experience serves as a reminder that AI assistance, while powerful, still requires human oversight and safety measures.
